title: Sahasraśīrṣaṃ devam: the Nārāyaṇa hymn and the flame in the heart
theme: A hymn to Nārāyaṇa as the all, the highest light, brahman, the meditator and the meditation, followed by the place of meditation: the downward-facing lotus of the heart, the fire within it, and the supreme Self in the middle of its flame.

translation.literal: [Meditate on] the thousand-headed god, all-eyed, source of the world’s good; the all, Nārāyaṇa, the god, the imperishable, the highest abode; higher than the all, eternal, the all, Nārāyaṇa, Hari. This all is the Person; that [Person] lives on the all. [On] the lord of the all, lord of selves, everlasting, auspicious, unfallen; Nārāyaṇa, the great one to be known, the self of all, the final refuge. Nārāyaṇa [is] the highest light; the self [is] Nārāyaṇa, the highest. Nārāyaṇa [is] the highest brahman; the reality [is] Nārāyaṇa, the highest. Nārāyaṇa [is] the highest meditator; the meditation [is] Nārāyaṇa, the highest. And whatever in this world is seen or heard —
translation.readable: Meditate on the god with a thousand heads and eyes everywhere, from whom the world’s good comes: Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, the highest goal, beyond everything, eternal, Hari. This whole world is that Person, and that Person lives in it. He is the lord of all, the lord of every self, everlasting, kindly, unfailing; the great one to be known, the self of all, the last refuge. Nārāyaṇa is the highest light and the self; the highest brahman and the real; the one who meditates and the meditation. And whatever is seen or heard in the world —

translation.literal: — Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that, within and without. [Meditate on] the endless, undecaying seer, the end in the ocean, the source of the world’s good. The heart, like a lotus bud, facing downward, stands below the throat, at the end of a span above the navel. [It] shines, filled with garlands of flame, the great abode of the all. Covered all round with [channels] (śilābhiḥ), it hangs like a bud. Near it is a fine hollow; in that all is established. In its middle is a great fire with flames on every side, facing every way. He, eater of what comes first, stands distributing the food, unageing, wise; his rays spread sideways, upward, downward. It heats its own body from the soles to the head. In its middle a tongue of flame stands, very fine, rising upward, shining like a streak of lightning in a dark rain-cloud, thin as the awn of wild rice, yellow, bright, like an atom. In the middle of that flame the supreme self is placed. He [is] Brahmā, he Śiva, he Hari, he Indra; he the imperishable, supreme, self-ruling.
translation.readable: — Nārāyaṇa pervades it all, inside and out. Meditate on him: endless, undecaying, wise, the far shore of the ocean of the world, the source of its good. The heart, like a lotus bud turned downward, lies a span below the throat and above the navel. It shines, wreathed in flames: the great dwelling of all things. Hung about with channels, it hangs like a bud; near it is a fine opening in which everything rests. In it burns a great fire with flames on every side, facing every way, eating the food that comes to it and sending it through the body, never ageing, wise; its rays spread in all directions, and it warms the whole body from head to foot. In the middle of that fire is a thin flame rising upward, bright as lightning in a dark cloud, fine as the tip of a grain of wild rice, golden, minute. In the middle of that flame dwells the supreme Self. He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra; he is the imperishable, the highest, ruling by himself.

syntax: The first unit is a string of accusatives describing the god, with no verb of its own: the commentators supply ‘meditate on’ (dhyāyet). Short nominal sentences follow, each with nārāyaṇa(ḥ) and para: Nārāyaṇa is the highest light, brahman, meditator. The relative clause yac ca kiṃcij jagat … closes in the second unit with its main clause, antar bahiś ca tat sarvaṃ vyāpya nārāyaṇas sthitaḥ. The second unit then turns from praise to description: a chain of short statements, each anchored by tasya (‘of it’) or tasyāḥ (‘of that [flame]’), moves inward from the heart to the hollow, the fire, the flame and the Self, and ends in a list of identifications with saḥ.

ambiguities.note: viśvam evedaṃ puruṣas tad viśvam upajīvati. The anonymous commentator: the supreme self relies on the world for its activity, «स च परमात्मा तद्विश्वमुपजीवति, स्वस्य व्यवहारनिर्वाहार्थमाश्रयति». Bhāskara reverses it: the world lives on the Person, «इदं विश्वं पुरुष एव पूरयिता पुरुषस् तत् तस्माद् विश्वं जगत् पुरुषम् उपजीवत्य् आत्मानं लभते तत्परिणामत्वाद्विश्वस्य».
Read with the visarga restored (‘Nārāyaṇa is the highest …’, the anonymous commentator) or as a compound nārāyaṇa-para, ‘dependent on Nārāyaṇa’ (Bhāskara); see morphology.

For the anonymous commentator the flame is the finest tongue of the bodily fire, in which the supreme Self dwells. Bhāskara takes the flame-like thing as the individual self (jīva): «तस्य अग्नेर् मध्ये वह्निशिखासदृशो जीवो व्यवस्थितः», and the supreme Self as dwelling within it, contracted to its measure: «तस्यास् तादृश्या वह्निशिखाया मध्ये परमात्मा आत्मप्रकृतिभूतो नारायणो व्यवस्थितः, जीवानुरोधेन सङ्कुचितस्तिष्ठति».

The base and the Ānandāśrama text read śilābhiḥ (‘with stones’), which makes little sense; the Tirupati text and Bhāskara read sirābhiḥ (‘with veins, channels’), and the anonymous commentator explains śirābhiḥ as nāḍīs: «तञ्च शिराभिर्नाडीभिः».

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Bhāskara: «सहस्त्रशीर्षमित्याद्याः पञ्चानुष्टुभः ॥ तत एका द्विपदा । शिष्टं ब्राह्मणमानुष्टुभम् । अन्ते एका द्विपदा» — five anuṣṭubhs, a two-pāda verse (anantam avyayam, «इयं द्विपदा गायत्री»), the rest a brāhmaṇa in anuṣṭubhs, and a closing two-pāda verse (sa brahma …). The lines count 15, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16 in the first unit and 16, 17, 16, 16, 16, 15, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 15, 19 in the second.

beginner: This is one of the most widely recited passages of the Mahānārāyaṇa, often called the Nārāyaṇa Sūkta. It begins by praising Nārāyaṇa: he has a thousand heads and eyes everywhere, he is the source of the world’s good, the imperishable, the highest goal. Everything is that Person. He is the highest light, the highest reality, even the one who meditates and the meditation itself, and he fills whatever is seen or heard, inside and out. Then the hymn tells where to look for him: in the heart, which it pictures as a lotus bud hanging downward, a span above the navel. In the heart burns a great fire — the warmth that digests food and keeps the body warm — and in that fire a tiny flame, thin as the tip of a grain of rice and bright as lightning in a dark cloud. In the middle of that flame lives the supreme Self, who is called Brahmā, Śiva, Hari and Indra. The commentators read this as a guide to meditation.
analogy: Like a series of nested boxes, each opened in turn: the body, the heart, the fire, the flame — and at the centre, what all the boxes were made to hold.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It praises Nārāyaṇa as thousand-headed, all-eyed, the imperishable, the highest abode, the all, the Person on whom the all depends, the lord of selves, the highest light, brahman, the meditator and the meditation, pervading all that is seen or heard. Then it locates him: in the downward-facing lotus of the heart, in the fire within it, in the fine flame at the fire’s centre, where the supreme self dwells, who is Brahmā, Śiva, Hari, Indra, the imperishable, supreme and self-ruling.

commentary.q: How does it connect with what precedes?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the previous anuvāka ended with the form of the Great Lord to be meditated on in the lotus of the heart; here its qualities are set out at length: «पूर्वानुवाकान्ते ह्रदयपुण्डरीक उपास्यं यन्महेश्वरस्वरूपं निर्दिष्टं तस्मिन्नुपास्यगुणविशेषा अस्मिन्ननुवाके विस्तरेण प्रदर्श्यन्ते». Bhāskara: here too the supreme self is praised, «अत्रापि परमात्मा स्तूयते».

commentary.q: What does the name Nārāyaṇa mean?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator cites a verse which he says the Purāṇas give: «आपो नारा इति प्रोक्ता आपो वै नरसूनवः» — the waters are called nārāḥ, and they were his first dwelling; reported as cited by him. Bhāskara derives it from nara, the leader, whose own are the nārāḥ, of whom he is the ground: «नरः नेता सर्वस्य स्वामी तस्य स्वभूताः पशवो नारास् तेषाम् अयनम् उपादानं नारायणम्».

commentary.q: Is the Self here a particular form?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator denies it: Nārāyaṇa himself is the self, not some other embodied form, «अतो नारायणः एवाऽऽत्मा न त्वपरो मूर्तिविशेषः». On the closing list he says the Self, though dwelling in a small place for the sake of meditation, is not small but all the gods, «तस्योपासनार्थमल्पस्थानत्वेऽपि न स्वयमल्पः किंतु सर्वदेवात्मकः», and supreme as free of māyā, «परमो मायारहितः शुद्धश्चिद्रुपः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: like the hollow of an eight-petalled lotus, but facing down where an ordinary lotus faces up, «लौकिकं पद्ममूर्ध्वाभिमुखं»; below the base of the neck, «निष्टिर्ग्रीवाबन्धस्तस्या अधस्ताद्वर्तते», a span of twelve finger-breadths above the navel. The fire in it he identifies with the digestive fire, quoting the Gītā’s «अहं वैश्वानरो भूत्वा प्राणिनां देहमाश्रितः», and its warmth with the body’s: «सोऽयं शरीरगतः संतापोऽग्निसद्धावे लिङ्गम्».

commentary.q: How do the commentators read the flame?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: For the anonymous commentator the flame is the finest tongue of that fire, with the supreme self in its midst: «तस्याः पूर्वोक्ताया वह्निशिखाया मध्ये जगत्कारणभूतः परमात्मा विशेषेणावस्थितः». Bhāskara reads the flame as the individual self, with Nārāyaṇa dwelling within it, contracted to its measure: «तस्य अग्नेर् मध्ये वह्निशिखासदृशो जीवो व्यवस्थितः». The anonymous commentator thus places the supreme self directly in the flame, Bhāskara within the jīva.

commentary.q: What is the purpose of the description?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the meaning of the whole is that one should meditate on the god described from sahasraśīrṣam on, in the manner described from padmakośapratīkāśam on: «सहस्त्रशीर्षमित्यादिवाक्यप्रतिपादितं पद्मकोशप्रतीकाशमित्यादिवाक्योक्तप्रकारेण ध्यायेदिति तात्पर्यार्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Several places differ: nārayaṇaḥ in the base against nārāyaṇaḥ in the Ānandāśrama text; śilābhiḥ against sirābhiḥ (Tirupati, Bhāskara); jvālamālā- against jvālāmālā- (Ānandāśrama); padam against prabhum (Tirupati, which Bhāskara also comments on); and in the last line the Tirupati text has brahmā. Bhāskara’s text has no ‘sa hariḥ’: «स एव ब्रह्मा स एव स्रष्टा स एव शिवः रुद्रः स एव इन्द्रः देवराजः». Sāyaṇa’s comment on this anuvāka is not in the edition’s copy.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here, and Sāyaṇa’s comment on this anuvāka is missing from the copy used). The anonymous commentator speaks in Advaita terms (the world superimposed on its ground, the self free of māyā); Bhāskara reads the flame as the individual self within which the supreme self dwells. Neither is presented here as the meaning of the text.

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka says the same in the other order: the Person is all this.
The Chāndogya’s small lotus-dwelling in the city of brahman, the space within the heart to be sought.
The hundred and one channels of the heart, which the anonymous commentator quotes for the channels round the heart.
The anonymous commentator quotes this verse for the fire in the heart that digests food.
The anonymous commentator quotes this verse to explain akṣara in the last line.

contemporary.text: The hymn moves from the vastest image, a god with a thousand heads, to the smallest, a flame thin as a grain’s awn, and says they are the same. Turning attention from the very large to the very near is a familiar discipline in many traditions of contemplation. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a hymn describe the same god as vast and as tiny?
reflect.deeper: The commentators disagree on whether the world depends on the Person or the Person on the world. What follows from each reading?
reflect.practice: Sit quietly and notice the warmth of your own body for a minute, without naming it.

references.text: This anuvāka is Bhāskara’s anuvāka 11 (his comment covers both units). Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 11–12, which would correspond, are missing from the edition’s copy.
The Nambūtiri (Kerala) recitation of this hymn is preserved in the vishvAsa sources as a separate text; it is not collated here.

flags.note: nārayaṇaḥ (base) against nārāyaṇaḥ (Ānandāśrama text); śilābhiḥ (base, Ānandāśrama) against sirābhiḥ (Tirupati; Bhāskara’s sirābhiḥ, the anonymous commentator’s śirābhiḥ); jvālamālā- against jvālāmālā-; padam against prabhum (Tirupati). All classed on the sources page.
Bhāskara’s text lacks ‘sa hariḥ’ in the last line and reads vitastyāṃ tu for vitastyānte.
sendraḥ (saḥ + indraḥ) needs the sandhi engine to join saḥ with a following vowel (the rule of P. 6.1.134 (सोऽचि लोपे चेत्‌ पादपूरणम्)); reported as a shared-code need.
The commentators supply ‘meditate on’ for the accusatives of the first lines; the text has no verb there.
